newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian rupiah swings on currency control fears.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian rupiah swings on currency control fears.

text.p: The Indonesian rupiah took a roller-coaster ride on Friday amid fears that the central bank would take measures to control speculation.
The rupiah soared to a high of 2,413 to the dollar from an opening of 2,444.0/45.0 on rumours that the central bank would cancel swap facilities for overseas investors.
The rumours drew strength from the fact that authorities in Thailand had used the move to quell a run on the baht.
But the rupiah calmed after Bank Indonesia denied ht had any such plan and had slipped back to 2,440.0/43.0 by mid-afternoon.

Bambang Trianto, director of the central bank's foreign exchange department, told Reuters the bank had no plan to mirror Thailand by asking banks to stop quoting tomorrow/next swaps to offshore investors.
"We have no intention to freeze the swap facility for now," Trianto said. "But we are watching the market very closely.
"We are comfortable with market rates," Trianto said.

Swaps, simultaneous purchases and sales of identical amounts of one currency for another with two different value dates, are an essential instrument for foreign investors to hedge currency exposures or to obtain domestic liquidity.
The Bank of Thailand squeezed players speculating that the Thai baht would be devalued following a slow-down in the economy by asking Thai banks to stop quoting tomorrow/next swaps.
The move means foreigners have to pay high prices to obtain domestic currencies to finance their speculation.

Saleh Aziz, treasury manager at Bank Export-Import Indonesia, said foreign players swamped the local swap market in the morning on fears that Bank Indonesia could follow Thailand amid rumours that Malaysia's Bank Negara had done the same.
The Malaysian central bank also denied it was planning any such move.

"Liquidity is the key to the market," Aziz said, adding that offshore investors had built up heavy long dollar positions since the campaign for Indonesia's May 29 general elections started more than two weeks ago.
Offshore investors were getting nervous about the election campaign because of sporadic violence, dealers said, although they added that the violence was minor.

The rumours about currency restrictions led to offshore players swamping the swap market, driving tom/next to a high of seven points, equivalent to about 100 percent interest, before they fell to 0.6/0.7 points.
One-month swaps soared to a high of 50 points, equivalent to some 31 percent, before cooling off to 24.0/28.0 points.
"I think the rupiah is affected more by a spill-over from speculation in the ringgit," one dealer in Singapore said.

"Many who went long on dollars on Thursday got burnt today. It's really a wild swing. I had one screen quoting swaps at 30 (points) while the other screen was at 60. There were a lot of arbitrage opportunities," the dealer said.
Aziz said he expected swap premiums to fall gradually because the central bank would not be happy to live with such an expensive rate, considering its plan to contain inflation.
